newsitem.title: USA: Chance of fog delays U.S. shuttle landing.
newsitem.headline: Chance of fog delays U.S. shuttle landing.

text.p: The crew of the space shuttle Discovery got an extra day in orbit on Monday after a forecast for fog foiled their landing plans.

The $2 billion reusable spaceship had been scheduled to return to Earth shortly after sunrise on Monday, but forecasters were concerned that the runway at the Kennedy Space Center would be obscured by fog.
"The probability of fog is too high to be acceptable," mission control's Dom Gorie told the astronauts moments before they were due to begin their descent.
As it turned out, the predicted fog never materialized and blue skies would have greeted the returning astronauts.
Mission control rescheduled the landing for 7:08 a.m. EDT (1108 GMT) on Tuesday, but did not rule out the possibility of a predawn touchdown at 5:35 a.m. EDT (0935 GMT).
NASA officials had hoped to avoid a landing in darkness because of the extra risk involved, but said they might take the earlier option if the weather again looked uncertain.
Discovery's backup landing strip at Edwards Air Force Base in California would not be considered on Tuesday because of the additional $900,000 cost of transporting the orbiter back to Florida.
The shuttle had enough fuel and supplies to stay aloft until Thursday, but would probably return to Earth on one coast or the other by Wednesday, flight director Wayne Hale said.

Discovery's crew of six were enjoying their extra day aloft watching the Earth speed by 160 miles (256 km) below. Scientists took advantage of the extra day by reactivating several experiments in the shuttle's cargo bay.
"We'll definitely enjoy the day up here," shuttle commander Curt Brown said.
The crew, which includes a Canadian guest researcher, were to return to Earth with an atmospheric satellite carrying a bounty of information on the health of the Earth's protective ozone layer.
During the busy mission, the astronauts tested a Japanese prototype space station robot arm, grew colon cancer cells for medical research, and pointed a telescope at the receding comet Hale-Bopp.
Meanwhile at the Kennedy Space Center, the space shuttle Atlantis was hauled to its seaside launch pad on Monday for a planned late-September blastoff to Russia's Mir space station.
